techniques.definition: The dolly zoom, also called zolly or Vertigo effect, simultaneously dollies and zooms in opposite directions, creating a disorienting depth distortion where the subject stays the same size but the background appears to stretch or compress. Hitchcock pioneered this unsettling technique in Vertigo.

techniques.name: Follow Shot
techniques.definition: A follow shot tracks the subject laterally or from behind as they move through a scene, pursuing them through space. This technique maintains continuous connection with moving characters, creating immersion as viewers travel alongside the action rather than observing from a fixed position.

techniques.name: Jib Shot
techniques.definition: A jib shot uses an arm-mounted camera for sweeping arc movements, combining vertical and horizontal motion in fluid curves. Jibs are smaller than cranes and allow precise, controlled movements ideal for dynamic reveals, dramatic swoops, and following action in confined spaces.

techniques.name: Pedestal Shot
techniques.definition: A pedestal shot moves the camera straight up or down without tilting, as if rising or lowering on an elevator. Unlike tilts which angle the camera, pedestal moves maintain the same viewing angle while changing height, useful for revealing tall subjects or descending to details.

techniques.name: Smooth Tracking Shot
techniques.definition: A smooth tracking shot follows the subject fluidly without jerks or shakiness, gliding alongside movement with perfect stability. Whether using dollies, sliders, gimbals, or Steadicam, the goal is invisible camera movement that feels natural and keeps focus on the subject's journey.

techniques.name: American Shot
techniques.definition: The American shot, also called 3/4 shot or medium-long shot, frames subjects from approximately mid-thigh up. Developed in Hollywood westerns to show holstered guns while maintaining facial expressions, this framing balances body language with character emotion, ideal for action and group dynamics.

techniques.name: Full Shot
techniques.definition: A full shot frames the entire human body from head to toe, showing the complete figure within the environment. This framing reveals body language, costume, and physical action while maintaining enough distance to establish spatial context and character relationships.

techniques.name: Head Shot
techniques.definition: A head shot frames the subject from shoulders up, focusing on facial features in a portrait-style composition. Common in interviews, auditions, and character introductions, this tight framing emphasizes performance and expression while eliminating environmental distractions.

techniques.name: Italian Shot
techniques.definition: The Italian shot is an extreme close-up focusing only on the eyes, named for its prominence in Sergio Leone's Spaghetti Westerns. This intensely tight framing captures micro-expressions and creates powerful tension during standoffs or emotional peaks, making eyes the entire frame.

techniques.name: Profile Shot
techniques.definition: A profile shot captures the subject from the side, showing the face in pure profile silhouette. This classical framing emphasizes facial contours, creates elegant compositions, and can establish character relationships when two profiles face each other or look in the same direction.

techniques.name: Reverse Angle
techniques.definition: A reverse angle cuts to the opposite viewpoint in a scene, typically showing what a character was looking at or switching between conversation participants. This fundamental editing technique maintains spatial relationships while providing visual variety and coverage.

techniques.name: Shot-Reverse-Shot
techniques.definition: Shot-reverse-shot is a sequence alternating between two characters, typically during dialogue, showing each person's reactions to the other. This fundamental technique of narrative filmmaking creates conversational rhythm and allows editors to control pacing and emotional emphasis.

techniques.name: Trunk Shot
techniques.definition: A trunk shot frames the scene from inside a car trunk looking up at characters, creating an unusual low-angle perspective associated with crime films. Popularized by Quentin Tarantino, this distinctive angle places viewers in a vulnerable position, often revealing captives or bodies.

techniques.name: Wide Shot
techniques.definition: A wide shot captures the full scene including substantial environment around the subjects, establishing spatial relationships and context. Wider than a long shot, this framing emphasizes setting over character, useful for landscapes, architecture, and epic battle sequences.

techniques.name: Accent Light
techniques.definition: An accent light focuses illumination on a specific area or object for emphasis, drawing viewer attention to important props, details, or features. This targeted lighting separates key elements from the background and creates visual hierarchy within the frame.

techniques.name: Cucoloris
techniques.definition: A cucoloris (or cookie) is a board with irregular holes that creates patterned shadows when light passes through it. Used to simulate window blinds, tree branches, or abstract patterns, cookies add texture and visual interest to otherwise flat surfaces and backgrounds.

techniques.name: Diffusion
techniques.definition: Diffusion softens harsh light by passing it through translucent material like silk, muslin, or frosted filters. This technique reduces sharp shadows, minimizes skin imperfections, and creates gentle, flattering illumination commonly used in beauty, romance, and dream sequences.

techniques.name: Firelight
techniques.definition: Firelight creates warm, flickering orange illumination that dances across subjects, evoking campfires, candles, or hearths. This practical lighting effect suggests intimacy, survival, storytelling moments, and primitive settings, with its characteristic movement adding life to scenes.

techniques.name: Frontal Lighting
techniques.definition: Frontal lighting positions the main light source directly in front of the subject, aligned with the camera. This flat, shadowless illumination eliminates depth and dimension, creating even exposure useful for beauty shots, fashion, and deliberately stylized flat aesthetics.

techniques.name: Hair Light
techniques.definition: A hair light, also called back light or separation light, illuminates the subject's hair and shoulders from behind to create a rim of light that separates them from the background. This halo effect adds depth, dimension, and a polished professional quality to portraits.

techniques.name: Mood Lighting
techniques.definition: Mood lighting prioritizes emotional atmosphere over realistic illumination, using color, intensity, and placement to evoke specific feelings. Whether romantic candlelight, tense shadows, or ethereal glows, mood lighting manipulates viewer emotions through deliberate lighting choices.

techniques.name: Neon Lighting
techniques.definition: Neon lighting uses vibrant, glowing tubes or LED equivalents to create bold, saturated color environments. Associated with urban nightlife, cyberpunk aesthetics, and modern noir, neon's electric pinks, blues, and purples create striking, stylized atmospheres with high visual impact.

techniques.name: Rim Lighting
techniques.definition: Rim lighting places light sources behind subjects to illuminate their edges and outline, creating a glowing border that separates them from the background. This dramatic technique emphasizes silhouettes, adds production value, and creates angelic or heroic visual associations.

techniques.name: Top Lighting
techniques.definition: Top lighting positions the main light source directly overhead, casting shadows downward on the face and body. This dramatic angle creates skull-like shadows under eyes and nose, useful for horror, villains, interrogation scenes, and oppressive atmospheres.

techniques.name: Underwater Lighting
techniques.definition: Underwater lighting creates the distinctive blue-green, diffused illumination of subaquatic environments. Light refracts and scatters through water, producing caustic patterns, reduced visibility, and ethereal quality that transforms ordinary scenes into mysterious aquatic worlds.

techniques.name: Volumetric Lighting
techniques.definition: Volumetric lighting makes light beams visible as they pass through atmosphere containing fog, dust, smoke, or haze. These god rays or light shafts create dramatic depth, spiritual atmosphere, and three-dimensional illumination that sculpts space with visible light.

techniques.name: Anamorphic Flares
techniques.definition: Anamorphic flares are horizontal streaks of light caused by bright sources hitting anamorphic lenses. These distinctive blue or orange streaks across the frame have become associated with cinematic production value, adding stylized glamour and sci-fi aesthetics to images.

techniques.name: Bloom Effect
techniques.definition: Bloom creates a soft glow around bright areas where light appears to bleed beyond its boundaries. This overbright halation effect simulates how eyes and cameras perceive intense light sources, adding dreamy, ethereal, or heavenly qualities to illuminated areas.

techniques.name: Chromatic Aberration
techniques.definition: Chromatic aberration produces color fringing at high-contrast edges, where red-green or blue-yellow halos appear due to lens imperfections. Once considered a flaw, this effect is now deliberately added for vintage, lo-fi, or psychedelic aesthetics.

techniques.name: Color Correction
techniques.definition: Color correction adjusts footage to achieve accurate, consistent color representation, fixing white balance issues, matching shots, and ensuring skin tones appear natural. This technical process precedes creative color grading and establishes a neutral baseline for further stylization.

techniques.name: Crossfade
techniques.definition: A crossfade smoothly blends two shots by simultaneously fading one out while fading the next in, creating a momentary overlap. This gentle transition suggests the passage of time, connects related scenes, or creates dreamy, ethereal connections between images.

techniques.name: Glow Effect
techniques.definition: A glow effect adds soft luminosity around bright objects, lights, or highlights, creating an ethereal, magical quality. Used for supernatural elements, heavenly visions, and romantic atmospheres, glow suggests otherworldly radiance and visual warmth.

techniques.name: HDR Effect
techniques.definition: HDR (High Dynamic Range) effect maximizes detail in both highlights and shadows simultaneously, creating images with expanded tonal range. This technique reveals detail in bright skies and dark shadows that would normally be lost, producing hyper-detailed, sometimes surreal results.

techniques.name: Loop Animation
techniques.definition: Loop animation creates seamlessly repeating motion that cycles infinitely without visible start or end points. Used for backgrounds, ambient elements, and hypnotic effects, perfect loops require careful planning to ensure the end frame transitions invisibly to the beginning.

techniques.name: Motion Blur
techniques.definition: Motion blur adds realistic streaking to moving elements, simulating how cameras capture movement during exposure. This effect conveys speed, urgency, and kinetic energy while smoothing animation and making fast motion feel natural rather than strobing.

techniques.name: Parallax Effect
techniques.definition: Parallax creates depth by moving visual layers at different speeds—distant elements move slowly while closer ones move quickly. This 2.5D technique transforms flat images into dimensional environments, adding cinematic depth to photographs and creating immersive scrolling effects.

techniques.name: Particle Effects
techniques.definition: Particle effects simulate collections of small elements like sparks, rain, snow, dust, embers, or magical energy. These dynamic systems add environmental atmosphere, magical elements, and physical phenomena that bring scenes to life with natural or fantastical motion.

techniques.name: Reflections
techniques.definition: Reflections capture mirror-like surfaces showing the environment, adding realism, depth, and visual complexity to scenes. Whether in water, glass, chrome, or wet pavement, accurate reflections ground images in physical reality and double visual information.

techniques.name: Refractions
techniques.definition: Refractions show light bending as it passes through transparent materials like glass, water, or crystals, distorting the view behind them. This optical effect adds scientific accuracy, magical qualities, and visual interest to translucent objects and liquid surfaces.

techniques.name: Vignette
techniques.definition: A vignette darkens or desaturates the edges of the frame, drawing viewer focus toward the brighter center. This classic photographic effect, originally a lens artifact, creates intimate focus, vintage aesthetics, and natural eye-line guidance within compositions.

techniques.name: Vintage Film Look
techniques.definition: The vintage film look recreates characteristics of aged analog footage including grain, scratches, light leaks, color fading, and gate weave. This nostalgic aesthetic evokes specific eras, adds warmth and texture, and suggests memory or historical footage.

techniques.name: White Balance
techniques.definition: White balance adjusts color temperature to ensure neutral whites under different lighting conditions. Correcting for warm tungsten or cool daylight prevents unwanted color casts, while deliberate white balance shifts can create warm or cold emotional atmospheres.

techniques.name: Silent Slapstick
techniques.definition: Silent slapstick is the physical-comedy language of Chaplin, Keaton and Lloyd: wide, locked-off frames that keep the whole body and the whole gag visible. Undercranked motion, iris transitions, intertitles and pantomime acting replace dialogue entirely. The style prizes choreography, props and peril staged in real space.

techniques.name: Screwball Comedy
techniques.definition: Screwball comedy is the fast-talking romantic style of 1930s and 40s Hollywood — overlapping dialogue, battle-of-the-sexes plots and impeccable art-deco interiors. Photography is bright, glossy high-key black-and-white with elegant medium two-shots that keep sparring couples locked in the same frame.

techniques.name: Technicolor Musical
techniques.definition: The Technicolor musical is the saturated three-strip look of golden-age Hollywood song-and-dance pictures. Candy-coloured soundstage sets, crane choreography and hard, even lighting make every hue vibrate at maximum intensity. The frame is wide, symmetrical and built around movement.

techniques.name: New Hollywood
techniques.definition: New Hollywood is the American cinema of the late 1960s and 70s: naturalistic light, zoom lenses, real locations and morally ambiguous antiheroes. Grainy Eastmancolor stock, loose handheld coverage and downbeat endings replaced studio gloss with documentary-inflected realism.

techniques.name: Conspiracy Thriller
techniques.definition: The 70s conspiracy thriller frames its characters as small figures dwarfed by architecture — long-lens shots across plazas, atriums and parking garages that imply constant surveillance. Muted colours, available light and telephoto compression build institutional paranoia into the composition itself.

techniques.name: Grindhouse
techniques.definition: Grindhouse recreates the battered look of 1970s exploitation double features: scratched emulsion, missing frames, burnt-out reel changes and oversaturated, badly timed colour. The style is deliberately trashy — lurid subject matter, snap zooms and jagged cuts worn like badges of honour.

techniques.name: Gothic Horror
techniques.definition: Gothic horror is the candlelit castle style of Universal and Hammer: fog-drenched graveyards, crumbling manors, velvet capes and lightning against painted skies. Rich, theatrical colour, deep shadows and romantic production design make dread feel opulent rather than gritty.

techniques.name: Body Horror
techniques.definition: Body horror stages the transformation, mutation or betrayal of flesh itself, in the tradition of Cronenberg and Carpenter. Clinical framing and unflinching macro detail meet practical prosthetics, latex and slime, with cold fluorescent or medical lighting that leaves nowhere to hide.

techniques.name: J-Horror
techniques.definition: J-horror is the Japanese ghost-film style of the late 1990s: pale spirits with long black hair, cursed technology and moisture everywhere. The palette is drained toward grey-green, interiors are dim and ordinary, and horror accumulates through stillness, negative space and glimpses at the edge of frame.

techniques.name: Southern Gothic
techniques.definition: Southern Gothic soaks decaying plantations, kudzu, revival tents and swampland in humid golden haze. Sweat, rust and rot texture every surface while beauty and menace share the frame — long magic-hour exteriors against interiors lit by single practical lamps.

techniques.name: Film Soleil
techniques.definition: Film soleil is noir relocated to blinding sunlight — desert highways, motel pools and mirrored aviators instead of rain and neon. Overexposed whites, hard black shadows and heat shimmer make daylight itself feel hostile and morally bleached.

techniques.name: Acid Western
techniques.definition: The acid western warps frontier iconography into hallucination: sun-flared landscapes, anachronistic drifters and death treated as psychedelic ritual. Expect high-contrast monochrome or bleached colour, extreme wide lenses and dream logic replacing plot logic.

techniques.name: Neo-Western
techniques.definition: The neo-western transplants frontier morality into the present day — pickup trucks instead of horses, border country instead of open range. Vast anamorphic landscapes dwarf laconic characters, with natural magic-hour light and long silences doing the storytelling.

techniques.name: Samurai Cinema
techniques.definition: Samurai cinema is the jidaigeki style of Kurosawa and Kobayashi: telephoto battle coverage, weather as drama — driving rain, dust, wind — and rigorous geometric blocking. Duels are held in long, tense stillness broken by a single decisive cut.

techniques.name: Heroic Bloodshed
techniques.definition: Heroic bloodshed is the Hong Kong action-melodrama style of John Woo: two-gun standoffs, doves, slow-motion dives and brotherhood pushed to operatic extremes. Muzzle flashes bloom in smoky warehouses while intercut close-ups turn gunfights into emotional arias.

techniques.name: Kaiju Cinema
techniques.definition: Kaiju cinema stages giant monsters against miniature cities in the Toho tradition. Low angles from street level sell impossible scale, searchlights rake smoke-filled night skies, and suitmation texture — rubber, sparks, collapsing model buildings — gives destruction a handmade weight.

techniques.name: Bollywood Masala
techniques.definition: Masala style blends romance, action and musical spectacle in one saturated package: costume changes mid-song, monsoon-soaked embraces, hundreds of synchronized dancers and crane shots that swirl around the leads. Colour is pushed to festival intensity and emotion is played at full volume.

techniques.name: Cinéma du Look
techniques.definition: Cinéma du look is the glossy 1980s French style of Besson and Beineix — youth, speed and doomed romance rendered in high-style images. Neon and primary colours slick wet streets, metro tunnels and brutalist interiors, with fashion-editorial composition prized over realism.

techniques.name: Magical Realism
techniques.definition: Magical realism treats the impossible as mundane: levitations, ghosts and miracles photographed with the same calm naturalism as breakfast. Warm practical light, unhurried camera moves and matter-of-fact staging let wonder infiltrate the everyday without fanfare.

techniques.name: Afrofuturism
techniques.definition: Afrofuturism fuses African aesthetics, diasporic history and speculative technology — chrome and cowrie shells, ancestral pattern and starship geometry in one frame. Rich melanin-forward lighting, regal costume design and cosmic colour palettes build futures rooted in heritage.

techniques.name: Cyberpunk
techniques.definition: Cyberpunk is high tech against low life: rain-slick megacity streets, holographic advertising, neon kanji and chrome prosthetics. Smoky shafts of light, teal-and-magenta glow and perpetual night render corporate dystopia as seductive spectacle.

techniques.name: Synthwave Retrowave
techniques.definition: Synthwave is the 1980s that never existed: gridded horizons, chrome text, VHS scanlines and a striped setting sun. Magenta-and-cyan gradients, sports-car silhouettes and analog glow render nostalgia as pure electric colour.

techniques.name: Steampunk
techniques.definition: Steampunk retrofits the future with Victorian machinery — brass goggles, airships, clockwork limbs and gaslit laboratories wreathed in steam. Warm tungsten and firelight play over copper, leather and rivets, giving fantasy technology a tactile, hand-built glow.

techniques.name: Space Opera
techniques.definition: Space opera is mythic adventure at galactic scale: vast capital ships crossing the frame, binary sunsets, throne rooms and cantina ensembles. Monumental production design, sweeping orchestral pacing and painterly nebula light favour grandeur over hard science.

techniques.name: Painterly Anime Pastoral
techniques.definition: The painterly anime pastoral, in the Studio Ghibli tradition, renders countryside light in gouache washes — cumulus towers, wind through grass, cluttered kitchens glowing at dusk. Compositions breathe with gentle detail and the resting beats between actions.

techniques.name: Stop-Motion Aesthetic
techniques.definition: The stop-motion aesthetic embraces the handmade: felt, clay and armature puppets animated frame by frame with visible fingerprints and slightly imperfect motion. Miniature depth of field and tungsten-warm practical sets give every scene a diorama intimacy.

techniques.name: Coming-of-Age Indie
techniques.definition: The coming-of-age indie look is soft natural light through bedroom curtains, bicycles at dusk, and 16mm-style grain over pastel suburbia. Handheld intimacy, sun flares and end-of-summer melancholy frame small moments as monumental.

techniques.name: Nordic Noir
techniques.definition: Nordic noir is the Scandinavian crime aesthetic: flat grey daylight, desaturated blues, knitwear and rain over concrete and fjord. Wide, still compositions hold bleak landscapes and unreadable faces, letting silence and cold negative space carry the tension.
